lead: A microwave integrated circuit (MIC) builds a whole microwave circuit as flat patterns on one substrate, so that every connection is a short, controlled transmission line. In a hybrid MIC the lines and passive parts are printed on a ceramic board and the transistors and diodes are attached afterwards. In a monolithic MIC (MMIC) every part, transistors included, is made inside one semiconductor wafer. Phones, radar modules, satellite receivers and 5G base stations use them because they are small, repeatable and still behave above 1 GHz.
prereq: You need: microstrip and coplanar lines, εeff and λg (see Microstrip, stripline and printed lines), and S-parameters.

sections.h3: Hybrid MIC: printed passives, mounted devices

blocks.text: In a hybrid MIC the substrate carries the passive pattern: microstrip or coplanar lines, couplers, filters, matching stubs and thin-film resistors. Transistors, diodes and chip capacitors are made separately, fixed by epoxy or solder, and joined to the pattern with short gold bond wires. Hybrids are easy to tune by trimming, handle more power, and are quick to prototype; but each bond wire adds about 1 nH per millimetre, which matters at high frequency.

items: Alumina (Al₂O₃): εr ≈ 9.8, hard, cheap and a good heat conductor; the usual hybrid substrate, 0.25 mm or 0.635 mm thick.
Fused silica (quartz): εr ≈ 3.8, very low loss, used for fine lines at millimetre waves.
PTFE laminates (εr about 2.2 to 3.5): soft board for low-cost hybrids.
LTCC (low-temperature co-fired ceramic): many thin layers, so buried striplines and 3-D passives fit inside one package.

blocks.text: Line geometry sets impedance: a microstrip of width w on height h and permittivity εr has an impedance Z₀ and an effective permittivity εeff between 1 and εr, because part of the field is in air; the guided wavelength is λg = λ₀/√εeff. Thin-film patterns (sputtered metal, photolithography) give fine, stable lines and resistors; thick-film printing is cheaper and coarser.

sections.h3: MMIC: the whole circuit in one wafer

blocks.text: A monolithic microwave integrated circuit forms transistors, resistors, capacitors, inductors and lines in or on one semi-insulating wafer, usually GaAs (resistivity above 10⁷ Ω·cm, εr = 12.9), also GaN on SiC for power, InP above 100 GHz, and silicon (RF-CMOS, SiGe) for high volume. One wafer run yields thousands of identical circuits with no bond wires inside them.

items: Transistor: MESFET or HEMT on GaAs and GaN; HBT on GaAs, InP or SiGe; MOSFET in RF-CMOS. Above its corner frequency a transistor's current gain falls about 6 dB per octave, so a device with 20 dB more gain than needed at 2 GHz has about none to spare at 20 GHz (3.3 octaves higher).
Resistor: thin film (NiCr or TaN) or the implanted active layer; R = Rs × (length/width), with Rs the sheet resistance in Ω per square.
MIM capacitor: metal, thin silicon nitride, metal; C = ε₀εrA/d. With εr = 7.5 and d = 0.2 µm it gives about 0.33 fF per µm², so values are a fraction of a pF to a few pF.
Spiral inductor: a flat metal spiral, a few nH at most; series metal resistance and substrate loss keep its Q near 10 to 20.

Airbridge: a thick plated metal strap (the second metal) that leaves the surface and crosses over another line or a spiral's turns with air beneath, so its crossing capacitance is small. Via holes through the thinned wafer connect top-side grounds to the back metal.

blocks.text: A typical GaAs process: form the active layer; isolate devices; make ohmic contacts and gates; deposit nitride and build MIM capacitors and resistors; pattern the first metal (lines, spiral turns, capacitor plates); plate the airbridge metal; thin the wafer to about 100 µm, etch back-side vias and metallise the back as ground.

Distributed lines are long on a chip. A 50 Ω microstrip on 100 µm GaAs has εeff ≈ 8.4, so a quarter-wave line at 10 GHz is 2.6 mm long and at 2 GHz 13 mm, larger than most chips. Below about 20 GHz MMICs therefore use lumped spirals and MIM capacitors for matching; above it, lines become short enough to use.

items: MMIC strengths: small, light, repeatable from chip to chip, broadband (no bond wires inside), and cheap per piece in volume.
MMIC limits: an expensive mask set and wafer run, no tuning after fabrication, low-Q passives, chip area costly, and power limited by heat in a thin die.
Hybrid MIC: higher power and Q, tunable, cheap tooling, quick to change; larger and less repeatable.

blocks.text: Packaging is part of the design. The die sits in a metal or ceramic package, connected by bond wires, flip-chip bumps or a coplanar launch to a connector. Bond wires add series inductance, and the package cavity must not resonate in the band: a cavity 15 mm by 15 mm has its first resonance near 14 GHz, so a 20 GHz chip needs a smaller cavity or absorber in the lid.

Test structures on the same wafer settle the process: a microstrip ring or half-wave resonator gives εeff from its resonant frequency and the loss from its Q. The finished chips are measured on-wafer with probes and a network analyser (see Microwave measurements). The amplifiers, mixers and oscillators built from these parts are treated in RF circuits and transceivers.

examples.question: A GaAs MMIC matching network needs (a) a 2 pF MIM capacitor using silicon nitride with εr = 7.5 and d = 0.2 µm, and (b) a 100 Ω thin-film resistor in a 50 Ω/□ film, 10 µm wide. Find the capacitor area and side, and the resistor length. (c) Compare with a quarter-wave line at 10 GHz on the same chip (εeff = 8.4).
steps: Capacitance per area: ε₀εr/d = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 7.5/0.2 × 10⁻⁶ = 3.32 × 10⁻⁴ F/m² = 0.332 fF/µm².
Area A = C/(ε₀εr/d) = 2 × 10⁻¹²/3.32 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.024 × 10⁻⁹ m² = 6024 µm², a square about 77.6 µm on a side.
Resistor: R = R<sub>s</sub> × (l/w), so l/w = 100/50 = 2 squares; l = 2 × 10 µm = 20 µm.
Quarter-wave line: λg = λ₀/√εeff = 30 mm/√8.4 = 10.35 mm; λg/4 = 2.59 mm.
The capacitor and resistor fit in less than 0.1 mm; the line is 2.6 mm long, which on a 2 mm chip would have to meander. That is why low-GHz MMICs match with lumped parts.
examples.answer: MIM capacitor 6024 µm² (about 78 µm square); resistor 20 µm long by 10 µm wide; a 10 GHz quarter-wave line is 2.59 mm long.

import math
e0=8.854e-12
A=2e-12*0.2e-6/(e0*7.5)
print(round(A*1e12), round(math.sqrt(A)*1e6,1), 100/50*10, round(30/math.sqrt(8.4)/4,2))

examples.question: An on-chip spiral of 2 nH has Q = 12 at 2 GHz. (a) Find its series resistance. (b) Placed in series in a 50 Ω line, what is |S₂₁| and the power lost in it? (c) A 0.5 mm bond wire (about 0.5 nH) joins a hybrid amplifier at 10 GHz: find its reactance.
steps: Series impedance Z = 2.09 + j25.13 Ω between 50 Ω ports: S₂₁ = 2Z₀/(2Z₀ + Z) = 100/(102.09 + j25.13); |S₂₁| = 100/105.1 = 0.951, that is 0.44 dB.

Power absorbed in R as a fraction of the available power: |I|²R/P<sub>available</sub> = 4Z₀R/|2Z₀ + Z|² = 200 × 2.09/105.1² = 0.038, so 3.8 % heats the spiral; the rest of the 0.44 dB is reflected by the mismatch.
Bond wire: X = 2π × 10 × 10⁹ × 0.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 31.4 Ω, more than half of 50 Ω, so it must be part of the matching design.
examples.answer: R = 2.09 Ω; |S₂₁| = 0.951 (0.44 dB), with 3.8 % of the power absorbed in the spiral; the bond wire is +j31.4 Ω at 10 GHz.

traps: Calling every flat microwave board an MMIC. It is monolithic only if the transistors are made in the wafer; a board with mounted transistors is a hybrid MIC.
Treating on-chip spirals as ideal. Their Q is only about 10 to 20, so matching networks built from them lose signal and add noise.
Using εr where εeff belongs. Microstrip λg = λ₀/√εeff, with εeff < εr because part of the field is in air.
Forgetting that bond wires and vias are inductors, about 1 nH per millimetre: 0.5 nH is already 31 Ω at 10 GHz.
Mixing up the airbridge and the first metal. The airbridge is the plated second metal that crosses over lines with air beneath; lines, spiral turns and lower capacitor plates are the first metal.

quiz.q: Expand MMIC and say what makes it monolithic.
quiz.a: Monolithic microwave integrated circuit: transistors, resistors, capacitors, inductors and lines are all formed in or on one semiconductor wafer, with nothing bonded on inside the circuit.

quiz.q: Name two MMIC substrate materials and one property of each.
quiz.a: Semi-insulating GaAs: εr = 12.9, resistivity above 10⁷ Ω·cm, hosts MESFETs and HEMTs. InP: used above 100 GHz. Silicon: cheap, high volume, for RF-CMOS and SiGe. GaN on SiC: high power, good heat conduction.

quiz.q: Why is coplanar waveguide convenient for a MMIC with many shunt elements?
quiz.a: The strip and both ground planes lie on the top surface, so a shunt element reaches ground directly, without a through-wafer via for each connection.

quiz.q: Find the area of a 1.5 pF MIM capacitor with εr = 7.5 and d = 0.2 µm.
quiz.a: C/A = 0.332 fF/µm², so A = 1500 fF/0.332 = 4518 µm², about 67 µm square.

quiz.q: An on-chip 2 nH spiral has Q = 12 at 2 GHz. Find its series resistance and explain the cost.
quiz.a: R = ωL/Q = 25.13/12 = 2.09 Ω. The signal current flows through it, so a matching network loses power; in a low-noise amplifier this loss at the input adds directly to the noise figure.

quiz.q: Why does a MMIC usually handle less power than a hybrid MIC with the same transistor type?
quiz.a: The die is small and thin, so heat has little area to spread through; the lines are narrow, so current density limits them; and the on-chip matching adds loss. A hybrid spreads heat into a thicker ceramic and uses wider lines.

quiz.q: Why is a microstrip ring resonator put on the wafer?
quiz.a: Its resonant frequency gives εeff of the real process and its Q gives the line loss, so the design values are checked before circuits are frozen.

beyond: GaN-on-SiC MMICs now give tens of watts at X-band, moving radar front ends from tubes to chips, and phones pack the switch, low-noise and power amplifiers into one module. Search for "MMIC process design kit" and "GaN MMIC power amplifier".
